lower-blood-pressure-with-lifestyle-chan.name: Lowering blood pressure with lifestyle changes
lower-blood-pressure-with-lifestyle-chan.headline: Lowering blood pressure with lifestyle changes: what the NHS and UK charities list
lower-blood-pressure-with-lifestyle-chan.summary: The NHS advises everyone with high blood pressure to make lifestyle changes, such as eating less salt, being more active and cutting back on alcohol.
keyPoints: The NHS says everyone with high blood pressure is advised to make healthy lifestyle changes, with or without medicine.
The NHS gives a limit of no more than 6g of salt a day for adults, and much of the salt people eat is already in everyday foods.
Blood Pressure UK advises at least five portions of fruit and vegetables a day, partly because they contain potassium.
The NHS also lists regular activity, losing weight if overweight, keeping alcohol low and stopping smoking.

body.heading: Do lifestyle changes matter if medicine is offered?
body.body:
The NHS says everyone with high blood pressure is advised to make healthy lifestyle changes. Whether medicine is needed as well depends on the blood pressure readings and on the person's risk of heart attack or stroke. NICE publishes a patient decision aid for adults, titled How do I control my blood pressure? Lifestyle options and choice of medicines.

The NHS lists the main changes as eating less salt, eating a healthy balanced diet, cutting back on alcohol and caffeine, being more active, losing weight if overweight and stopping smoking.

body.heading: What do the sources say about salt?
body.body:
The NHS advises adults to have no more than 6g of salt a day. The NHS says much of the salt people eat is already in everyday foods such as bread, breakfast cereal and ready meals. Blood Pressure UK says most people eat almost twice the recommended six grams a day.

The NHS salt page lists foods that are high in salt, such as bacon, cheese, stock cubes, soy sauce and salted nuts. When a label lists only sodium, multiplying the sodium figure by 2.5 gives the amount of salt. NICE recommends that clinicians encourage people to keep their dietary sodium intake low. Blood Pressure UK says salt substitutes made from potassium chloride can be high in potassium, so people with kidney problems or diabetes are advised to check with a doctor or nurse first.

body.heading: What about fruit, vegetables and potassium?
body.body:
Blood Pressure UK advises at least five portions of fruit and vegetables every day. It says they also contain potassium, which can help to balance the effects of salt. Canned, frozen and dried fruit and vegetables also count, and the charity advises choosing canned products without added salt or sugar. The British Heart Foundation explains that potassium helps the kidneys remove sodium from the blood and pass it out in urine.

The British Heart Foundation describes the DASH diet as a plan that trims sodium while raising potassium, calcium and fibre. It contains plenty of fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and low-fat dairy products, and is low in salt, saturated fat, sugary foods and alcohol. The British Heart Foundation advises getting potassium through food rather than supplements, as too much can be harmful.

body.heading: How do alcohol, weight and activity fit in?
body.body: The NHS advises against regularly drinking more than 14 units of alcohol a week, and says to spread drinking over three days or more. The NHS lists losing weight, if overweight, among the changes that can help lower blood pressure. The NHS advice is to be active regularly, with at least 150 minutes of exercise a week, and says moderate activity is enough.

body.heading: What else do the NHS pages mention?
body.body: The NHS also lists cutting back on caffeine and stopping smoking among the changes that can help. NHS dietitian fact sheets say supplements of calcium, magnesium or potassium are not recommended as a way to lower blood pressure. Sources do not all give the same figures, so the NHS pages are the ones used here for limits on salt and alcohol.

references.title: NICE: Hypertension in adults, guideline NG136
Blood Pressure UK: Fruit and vegetables and your blood pressure

protecting-your-hearing-from-loud-noise.name: Protecting your hearing from loud noise
protecting-your-hearing-from-loud-noise.headline: Protecting your hearing from loud noise: headphones, earplugs and warning signs
protecting-your-hearing-from-loud-noise.summary: The WHO and NHS sources say noise-related hearing loss is permanent but can be prevented, mainly by lowering volume, taking breaks and using ear protection.
keyPoints: The WHO says noise-induced hearing loss can be prevented through safe listening, although the damage is permanent.
NHS inform advises choosing headphones that block out more outside noise rather than turning up the volume.
Reusable musicians' earplugs reduce the volume of music without muffling it, according to an NHS trust leaflet.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears.

body.heading: Can loud noise cause permanent hearing loss?
body.body: The WHO says noise-induced hearing loss can be prevented by following safe listening, although the damage itself is permanent. Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust says that once the cochlea has been damaged no treatment or surgery can undo it. The WHO estimates that 1.1 billion young people worldwide could be at risk of hearing loss from unsafe listening practices. NHS inform says hearing loss often develops with age or is caused by repeated exposure to loud noise, and that it is possible to reduce the risk of noise-induced hearing loss.

body.heading: What do the sources say about headphones?
body.body: NHS inform advises choosing headphones that block out more outside noise rather than turning up the volume. The Royal Free London leaflet says noise-cancelling headphones can help because they remove the urge to turn the volume up to drown out outside noise. The WHO advises keeping the volume low, taking short listening breaks and, where possible, using carefully fitted noise-cancelling earphones. The WHO's recommendations for young people include limiting daily use of personal audio devices to less than one hour. The Royal Free leaflet advises keeping the volume modest and taking a short break from headphones each hour. The WHO notes that smartphone apps can help monitor listening levels.

body.heading: How do earplugs and earmuffs differ?
body.body: NHS leaflets describe earplugs and earmuffs as working by reducing the level of sound that reaches the ears. Earplugs are described as probably best for long-term use, while very high noise levels may call for high-attenuation earmuffs. The Royal Free leaflet says reusable musicians' earplugs lower the volume of music without muffling it. Torbay and South Devon audiology says ordinary pharmacy earplugs are often designed for swimming or background noise and may not protect against damaging noise. The WHO recommends wearing earplugs in noisy venues.

body.heading: What are the warning signs of too much noise?
body.body: It suggests moving away from loudspeakers at loud events and taking a break from the noise every 15 minutes. RNID warns of a risk of hearing damage after just 15 minutes in a nightclub playing music at an average of 100 decibels without earplugs. The WHO advises watching for signs of hearing loss, such as ringing in the ears or trouble hearing some sounds or conversations.

body.heading: When does a change in hearing need medical advice?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears, hearing that has worsened over days or weeks, or hearing loss with earache or discharge from the ear. It advises a routine GP appointment when hearing is getting gradually worse. Arrangements for hearing assessments vary by area, and some NHS audiology services ask for a referral from a GP.

references.title: WHO: Deafness and hearing loss, safe listening
Royal Free London: Looking after your hearing
RNID: How loud is too loud?

eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test.name: Eye tests: who gets a free NHS sight test
eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test.headline: Eye tests: what happens and who is entitled to a free NHS sight test in England
eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test.summary: The NHS says everyone should have regular eye tests, at least every 2 years, and lists who can have a free NHS sight test in England.
keyPoints: An optometrist checks vision and the health of the eyes, and can spot conditions such as glaucoma and cataracts.
The NHS says glaucoma develops slowly and is usually picked up at routine eye tests.
People aged 60 or over, people with diabetes or glaucoma, and under-16s are among those who qualify for a free NHS sight test in England.
The NHS lists sudden intense eye pain with a red eye, nausea and blurred vision as needing emergency care: call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: What happens at an eye test?
body.body:
An optometrist or ophthalmic practitioner examines the inside and outside of the eyes. The aim is to check vision and eye health and to spot conditions such as glaucoma, macular degeneration and cataracts. An ophthalmic practitioner can prescribe glasses or contact lenses, and a dispensing optician fits them. If necessary, the optician refers the person to a GP or a hospital eye clinic for further tests.

When glaucoma is suspected, the NHS says the first checks are quick and painless and include vision tests and measurements of the pressure inside the eye. If glaucoma is suspected, referral to an eye specialist called an ophthalmologist follows for further tests.

body.heading: Why have tests when vision seems fine?
body.body: The NHS says glaucoma develops slowly over many years and is usually picked up during routine eye tests. It says everyone should have regular eye tests, at least every 2 years. People at higher risk of glaucoma, for example those with a parent, brother or sister who has it, may be advised to have tests more often.

body.heading: Who can have a free NHS sight test in England?
body.body: The NHS lists people aged 60 or over, under-16s, and 16 to 18 year olds in full-time education among those who can have a free sight test. People registered as partially sighted or blind, and people diagnosed with diabetes or glaucoma, also qualify. The list also covers some people at risk of glaucoma, including some with a close relative who has been diagnosed; the age and other conditions are set out on the NHS page. The list also covers some people receiving certain benefits; the NHS page gives the details. Everyone else pays for a private test; the full list is on the NHS page. In Scotland the rules differ, and NHS inform says all NHS eye examinations are free for people who usually live in the UK.

body.heading: How often does the NHS pay for a test?
body.body: The standard entitlement is a test every 2 years. An earlier NHS test can be arranged if the optometrist considers it clinically necessary. A person who wants tests more often than the optometrist considers necessary pays for a private test. Optical vouchers, which help with the cost of glasses or contact lenses, have their own eligibility rules separate from free sight tests; the NHS page sets out who qualifies.

body.heading: Which eye symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: NHS trust information advises seeing an optician or GP about vision worries that are not sudden. Glaucoma can sometimes come on suddenly, with intense eye pain, a red eye, rainbow-coloured circles around lights, blurred vision, nausea or vomiting, and a headache. The NHS says these symptoms need emergency care, and directs people to call 999 or go to A&E.

references.title: NHS: Free NHS eye tests and optical vouchers
NHS: How often can I have a free NHS sight test?

how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.name: How to read food labels: traffic lights
how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.headline: How to read food labels: traffic light colours, per 100g figures and salt
how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.summary: Red, amber and green traffic light labels show whether a food is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt, and per 100g figures allow comparison.
keyPoints: Front-of-pack labels show whether a product is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt.
Red means high, amber medium and green low; energy is not colour-coded.
The colours are mainly based on 100g or 100ml, which makes comparing similar products easier than portion figures do.
When a label lists sodium, multiplying by 2.5 gives the salt content, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What do the traffic light colours mean?
body.body: Front-of-pack labels show whether a product is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt. Red means a high level of that nutrient, amber means medium and green means low. Guidance suggests choosing products with more green and amber and fewer red. Energy, shown in kilojoules and kilocalories, is not colour-coded.

body.heading: Should products be compared per 100g or per portion?
body.body: The colours are mainly based on the amount in 100g or 100ml of the food. Using the per 100g column makes it easier to compare the nutrient content of similar foods. Portion sizes are chosen by manufacturers and can differ, so per portion figures may not be comparable between products. A serving can be as small as one biscuit, so eating two means doubling the figures.

body.heading: What are reference intakes?
body.body: The percentages on front-of-pack labels are based on guidelines for how much of each nutrient and how much energy an average adult needs in a day. They show how much of that daily amount one portion supplies. Where a label has no colour coding, comparing the percentage of the reference intake in a portion is another way to compare foods.

body.heading: How is salt shown on a label?
body.body: Some labels give sodium rather than salt, and the NHS says multiplying the sodium figure by 2.5 gives the amount of salt. The NHS describes a food as high in salt when it has more than 1.5g of salt per 100g, and low when it has 0.3g or less per 100g. The NHS advises adults to have no more than 6g of salt a day.

body.heading: Are these labels compulsory?
body.body: Government guidance describes front-of-pack nutrition labelling in the UK as voluntary. The nutrition table on the back of the pack is mandatory. Labels therefore differ between products, and the per 100g figures are the common point of comparison.

references.title: Food Standards Agency: Check the label
GOV.UK: Front of pack nutrition labelling guidance
British Heart Foundation: Food labels explained
